utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you're tendering that into evidence and it will be marked as?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So it will be P2032.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 2032? Thanks. Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Then, Your Honours should have OTP statement dated 13 February, 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I don't have that. You will have to bear with me but -- but there is -- I had some problems with the office downstairs this morning and there is some lack of coordination. What I need is an extra copy of that. I know that it exists because that's why I wanted to go through this before. So if I could have a copy of that, please? You can bring the witness in, in the meantime. Yes, and that will be Exhibit number P?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Then there are four attachments, these are attachments to the statement dated 27 August, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And the first attachment is list of refugees from Bosanska Krupa, the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. All right. That's because I have it in B/C/S only. I don't have it in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I have to apologise but I double-checked the disclosure and everything was in order the moment it was leaving our office so I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. This is why I'm going through this because I know that there was some difficulties downstairs. Is this the document which starts with 00844665?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's going to be Exhibit P2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And then we will make the adjustments afterwards. And it consists of how many pages?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: B/C/S consists of two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two pages only, 665, 666, okay. Then there is another document, B/C/S as well, which has ERN number 00844667?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's going to be P20?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It will be P2035.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And it consists of how many pages?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It consists two pages as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And then I have another document which starts with ERN number 00844669.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this will be 2036, P2036?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it consists of how many pages?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You're asking me too much but the last page is 00844681.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 81, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's it. And the last attachment is according to what I have here, attachment which consists of two pages starting with 00844682.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Exactly two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It consists of two pages. This will P2037?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Exactly. And the last document is diary. We provided Your Honours again with B/C/S and English version. I don't know whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we have that. At least -- and the other one what happened is this: That my secretary obviously kept separate the B/C/S from the English and put the English version of the documents that you have just mentioned in another binder which I have just located now. So that problem is solved. You don't have to worry about it. The diary is here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So the diary will be marked as P2038.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it starts with ERN number, just to -- the English, according to --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The English should be 01101445.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Perfect. And this will be P20?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 2038. All right. Okay. Is that all?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We moved fast. Thank you. Yes. Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are going to start giving evidence very soon. I want just to put your mind at rest before you do so, that all the precautionary or protective measures that you have asked for via the Prosecution have been granted by this Trial Chamber. In other words, the first one being that you will not be referred to by your name at any given moment here, and you will instead be referred to by a -- by means of a pseudonym. In fact you are going to be known in this Tribunal and in these proceedings as BT55. That's the first thing I wanted to tell you. The second thing is that you have asked for possibly not to have your face seen outside this courtroom during the transmissions that take place. We have granted that. And if the camera is focused on you and the usher puts it on video mode, you will see exactly how others will be seeing you outside of this courtroom. That's the second protective measure that we have adopted. There will be times when you will be asked some questions which, upon answering, you will necessarily need to give information that would identify you. In those instances we will go into private session. You will hear us, hear me in particular saying we go now into private session. When we go into private session I would want to put your mind at rest that no one is hearing what is going on outside these four walls so that's why we go into private session sometimes so there may be questions which will expose your identity but those will be in private session. If we happen to be in open session, please try not to give any information yourself which could identify you. For example, you won't mention any relative of yours by name as a relative, as being a relative. You won't mention the street where you used to live because others would be able to identify you so please don't try to destroy all that we have tried to build around you to protect your identity. Having said that, the usher is going to give you a piece of paper with the text of a solemn declaration that you are required to make under the rules of this Tribunal, the solemn declaration is to the effect that in the course of your testimony, you will be telling us the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. It's the equivalent of an oath. So please proceed by reading that solemn declaration aloud and then we can start.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a chair. And Madam Richterova will be examining you in chief. She will be basing her questions mainly on the two statements that you gave to the Prosecution and I ask the usher to provide you with a copy of each straight away in your language, B/C/S, so that -- but before doing so you're going to be shown a piece of paper on which there is your name. Just have a look at it and tell me whether that is your name or not, just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let Mr. Cunningham see it. Right. Let us see it and Madam Richterova, in the meantime you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. This will be P2031 under seal. And only I want to mention that the previous exhibits have to be under seal as well, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All of them?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: All of them because in all of them the name of the witness is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes. So starting from the statements themselves?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Starting from Exhibit P232 -- this is the first statement, through attachments and diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Not 232, it's 2032.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: 2032, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So Exhibits P2032 to 2037, if I remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 2038, both numbers included, will -- are being admitted under seal. Or they will remain under seal. Yes, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, you were shown your statements yesterday. Did you manage to read them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The information you provided in these statements, including the correction in the second statement, the informations are -- the information are correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you have opportunity to read again your diary which you provided to the representative of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And also the information, do you still stand that the information you provided are correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure that the information is correct. But this is just a summary of everything that happened. I couldn't describe everything in detail. There was too much of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We have already heard information about the political development in your municipality and the events preceding the 21st of April, 1992 so I would like to direct your attention to the events which cross -- which followed 21st of April, 1992. As we already heard, there was lots of shooting on 21st of April and you stated in your statement that the town was attacked. Did you know at that time who attacked the town of Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. Let's pause here. Let's go into private session straight away. You see, you have made the first mistake. You have not taken my advice. You haven't heeded my words. We need to redact that paragraph, please, Madam Chuqing. When we are in open session, please try to avoid giving information about yourself that could reveal your identity. So sorry, Madam Richterova, these are the teething troubles so let's proceed slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go back to your question, we can go into open session now again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If you could tell us what did you learn about those who attacked the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: On that day, that is the 21st of April, and that was a Tuesday, the tensions in the town culminated. There was a state of total confusion. And sometime before noon, there was a large-scale movement of Serbian population. The Serbs moved out in great numbers for the second time. After 12.00 noon, I knew that there were negotiations taking part in town in order to avoid a conflict. There was a lot of tension in the air. Above the town one could already notice lines of troops. We already had information that trenches had been dug out, that the artillery had been put in place. From Bihac, from the command of the Yugoslav People's Army there, a representative was invited and he was supposed to take part in the peace talks which were staged in order to avoid an attack. On that day we also learned that an ultimatum was given and according to this ultimatum, if the town was not empty by 7.00 in the afternoon, an attack would ensue. Why? Because according to some sort of a strategy, the Serbian part of the authorities which already existed under the name of local commune of Jasenica, and they attended those negotiations from Jasenica, they did not want to stay in the town of Bosanska Krupa. These negotiations lasted up to 1700 hours. At that time, I was having lunch with my family. I did not flee the town. My neighbours, Serbs, a large number of them left the town. When I asked them why they were doing that, their answer was, "You'd better do it yourself if you want to save your hide."

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting, I'm going to object because the question was what did you learn about the attack and it's gone way beyond that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question was actually if you could tell us what did you learn about those who attacked the town. I think we could stop there and if you want to perfect or get more information from the witness, you can put specific questions, Madam Richterova. In the meantime, sir, may I give you one piece of what I consider to be good advice? You will be asked a lot of questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Both from Madam Richterova and from Mr. Cunningham. I know that you feel that you have a lot of information to you can give us. The thing is that your statements have been admitted into evidence so please try to answer the questions that are put to you as briefly as possible, and also answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. We are not interested in having more information than what is being asked out of you. All right? So please try to limit your answer to the question. And do not go beyond. Yes, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sir, if you could please, really just answer me what did you learn about those who attacked the town? Who were they? Just this information.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: The town was attacked by the Serb troops which were already deployed above the town, in the general area of the town. Everything was put in place before the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Everything was put in place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sir, I wanted information about Serb troops. Can you tell me, did you learn, did you know at that time or did you learn later, which unit they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: When it comes to the troops, we knew officially and from the stories that we heard as citizens, that there were -- there was a large number of Serbian troops above Krupa and that the attack would take place, the attacks started at 1745 hours. When the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am going to stop you because you are not following my instructions. The question was: What information do you have about these Serbian troops? Did you at any time come to know which unit they belonged to? So the answer is, if -- yes or no. And if it's yes, then what kind of -- what unit did they belong to? That's the simple question. The rest when it started is not being asked out of you -- from you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know which unit it was. We only knew it was the Serbian army up there, and that those were the men that had left Bosanska Krupa and villages but it was only the Serbian troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And I want to ask you one more question. You mentioned before that you heard some ultimatums. Can you tell us who gave the ultimatum and what kind of ultimatum it was? But again, very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Very well, then. The ultimatum that was given on that particular day by the Serbian authorities, from Jasenica, ordered for all the barricades that were in Krupa to be dismantled and for all the citizens to move out from the left bank of the river, across the bridge. That was the ultimatum. The border was established along the River Una. Those were the two facts contained in this ultimatum according to the information that I had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And when you state that all had to left -- to the left bank, was it all the inhabitants or did he or did the ultimatum refer to one particular ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: The ultimatum applied to Serbs. Muslims and parts of -- and some Croats who resided in Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to clear this because otherwise the transcript may become misleading later on. If we don't remember the facts correctly. The ultimatum applied to whom? Muslims and Croats only or also to Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It applied to Muslims and Croats only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's it. Move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We already heard the town was attacked. You were at home. At any point, did you see soldiers coming closer to the buildings in which you lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes. Once the attack started, there was horrendous shelling and from all sorts of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did at any point were your buildings searched by these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Not at that moment, not on that day. It was only when Krupa fell. That was on Wednesday. On Wednesday, when the troops, the Serb troops, entered the town, then Krupa was according to them liberated, and the first three came to us, they stopped in front of the building, they asked us to come down, they had white stripes on multi-coloured uniforms they were wearing. These were the troops from Sanski Most. They were active servicemen. They searched us. They asked us whether we had any arms there. They inspected our IDs and they told us that we were not allowed to leave our building until the following morning and that on the following morning somebody else would come and tell us what to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: One more question about this ultimatum. Have you heard any particular Serb politician who would made this ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes. On the radio. Now, which radio was it? Radio Petrovac or Bosanska Krupa? But whatever. On the radio, in the morning, after that first attack on the town, that ultimatum was repeated and Mr. Miroslav Vjestica repeated it directly, and we all waited to see what would be done and then he repeated once again that all Muslims had to move over to the left bank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The transcript -- Miroslav? What is his other -- the rest of his name? Miroslav?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vjestica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sir, at any point did you decide to leave your building with other people and go to other direction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes. That Wednesday, when the town was already occupied, if I may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And now I really want you to be very brief because everything is in your statement. I just want you to take chronologically what happened. So where did you want to go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: We decided that night to flee because there were already snipers there and so on, and we knew that we would be done away if we stayed, because there were snipers there so that we had decided that night to leave, to flee the next morning, around 6.00, Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Where, where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: So I started with my family. And we found out, following some kind of our strategy, that it would be best to flee towards the petrol pump that was in the centre. And that is what we decided and we crossed running and there were some 30, 35 citizens with me, behind that petrol pump but that column which was fleeing with me, we only had the basic change of underwear. We did not take any gold or anything, because we've assumed that --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sir -- sir, please, I ask you again, short answer, because then I am -- I am lost, the judges will be lost, just short answer. Where did you wanted --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Very well. We headed towards the centre so that we could cross the bridge to the left bank. Because that was the shortest way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you already said that there were about 30 or 35 of you. At any point did you meet any Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: We did. Right behind the petrol pump, there was a large-ish group of Serb soldiers, we did not see them immediately because they were in trenches because the town had been occupied that night, and at the second stage of our flight, a Serb soldier who was their commander, spoke to me, that is he recognised my name, and he stopped me and said, "You mustn't go anywhere from there because it's too dangerous. There is those other soldiers there, I mean from Sanski Most, and they will kill you off." And he directed us in the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So as stated in your statement, and in your diary, you -- you were taken towards Sujinovac; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And from Sujinovac you were taken to Jasenovac; it's correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And were you taken from Sujinovac to Jasenovac on a bus? Or did you walk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Some went on foot because it's in the woods and it's about 3 and a half kilometres from the town, and others were put on buses because the number of people was growing, and they took us to Jasenovac to put us in the school there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you arrived to Jasenovac, how were you treated? And now I'm talking, when you arrived on buses, when -- before you entered to school and after you entered the school.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: I'm sorry. First I think we are both making a mistake. It's not Jasenovac, it's Jasenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Jasenica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes, Jasenica. We got there at around 1400. We got off the bus in a column, in a single file and there was a reception desk at the junction and they took our names down and then took to us classrooms accommodating 30 to 35 citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: At any point, after your arrival to Jasenica, were you harassed or everything was in order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: As we were getting off the buses, because there was always -- there were always patrols of two escorting us everywhere and there was the reaction of citizens from children to the elderly, that is, they called us balija, they insulted us, swore at us, so those were this minor harassment and when we were moved to the classrooms then we were already protected from those soldiers by those who were in the corridors guarding us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When were you in these class rooms, did any officials came to see you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: In those classrooms, a threesome came to that classroom and we found out afterwards that they were kind of a court. It was Vojvoda Mitar Ciganovic, who was wearing an army uniform, and with him, the second one was Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you remember his first name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mladen Drljaca, Mladen, Mladja. He was the SDS secretary and had law -- a law degree. And the third one was Priest Ilija.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Priest Ilija addressed us first and he asked us if we were hungry, and on behalf of the group I said, since I knew him personally, I said, "Mr. Ilic" - that is what I said - "yes, we are hungry" and they promised to prepare some food for us because we had passed two days without eating anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: At any time during these three men were present, was your status discussed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes. After Priest Ilija, Mr. Mladjo as a lawyer addressed us and said that we should not be afraid, that we were in the shape of prisoners, but as refugees, as citizens, because we had not been captured with any weapons and he said that was a mitigating circumstance and that that we would be therefore accorded our own status in Jasenica. But shortly after that, Vojvoda Mitar Ciganovic addressed us and he said that we had to elect a body which would represent us in discussions with them, to elect a three-member body and that higher level they would discuss what would happen next, and that the rest should wait in the classroom. So we had in the beginning this lowest level of civilian prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said this lower level of civilian prisoners. Were you allowed to move after this discussion, were you allowed to move to another village? Or were you ordered to stay in Jasenica?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sir, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We need -- thank you, Judge Janu [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we need to redact this entire paragraph. Then we proceed going into private session. Please repeat your question or I will direct the witness myself to answer the same -- make the same statement but in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sir, were you allowed to go to another village? Your answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes. They allowed it. It was their decision, which village. So that there were two or three options. We couldn't adopt any -- you'd better kill us. That was the kind of talks that we conducted. So they chose the village of Arapusa.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the translation is very confusing. We couldn't adopt any -- you would better kill us. So I do not understand. Was there any place you didn't want to go? Or what is the reference to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes. The first thing they offered was the school at Benkovac, because I knew that place, and as a negotiator, I most emphatically gave this up and I said, "You better kill us than send us there because it's an unprotected place." And then they said they'd look into another option and then the recommendation came for the Arapusa neighbourhood community.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sir, you were allowed to go to Arapusa. Do you know whether anybody from Bosniaks stayed behind, stayed in Jasenica school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, there was another group and they were higher-ranking prisoners of sorts, about 22 of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Who --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: That was my question. In Arapusa, from your statement and your diary, it's obvious that you stayed there from 24 until 1st of May, when you were ordered to move to another place; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During these several days, you stated in your statement that some paramilitary group came to this village; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: It is. They were eagles, white.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What did they wear? What kind of uniform did they wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: They were that seven strong group which attacked the three of us in a car, they were wearing army uniforms and they looked like winter uniforms, grey, and they had the so-called stepas, caps, with a big, white eagle. As for weapons, they had knives in boots and three or four grenades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked about the uniform, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And sir, these White Eagles, did they come to your village? And how did -- yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And how did they treat the people in the village of Arapusa? And very briefly what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: They entered in that car and we went to seek medical aid, the three of them, because we were not allowed to move around Arapusa without permit, and we were moving towards the police station when they came up.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: The White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I only want to know what happened. Did they harass anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes. No sooner did they enter Arapusa then they attacked two or three houses and they injured two old women and they looted. When they fetched up next to us they surrounded us and they demanded money from us. Then since they found nothing on us, then they beat us with rifle butts and went on to the next houses and there a murder was committed. A woman was killed then.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In your statement and in your diary, you describe how Jasminka Causevic was killed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have here --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What was the name of the person? Because we have two names in your two statements, so could you please clarify the name of the person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Jasminka Causevic. That is her real surname.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a moment, Madam Richterova, because I think in all fairness this needs to be clarified. In your -- in one of your statements, the one of the 27th of August --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, I will explain to you. This name was corrected in the second statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not worried about that, the name of the woman that was killed allegedly. In this statement, you say -- you don't mention just one paramilitary group. You mention others. You mentioned the White Eagles, you mention the Red Berets and you also mentioned Seselj's men. What I want to know from you is, do you stand by your statement that these three paramilitary groups were present in this village at the same time or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Not at the same time. They came in groups on different days during those seven days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first ones that came from the White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And when this woman was killed, Jasminka, who according to you would be responsible out of these paramilitary groups? The White Eagles, the Red Berets or Seselj's men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The White Eagles, who had beaten us before that, and as soon as they left us lying on the ground, they rushed into that house. That wasn't far from us, only ten metres, or so. And they dashed into it and there were three individuals and then with an automatic rifle, one could hear loud fire. They used that automatic rifle to kill Jasminka. That other woman and the man were not killed. She was the only one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With regard to the Red Berets and Seselj's men, do you recall any activities by these paramilitary groups which could be of importance to us? While you were there, obviously.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were organising actions aimed at Bosanska Krupa. That is operations that had to do with the liberation, as they put it, of Bosanska Otoka and between 2.00 and 3.00 at night, two buses came --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you see them ill treat, maltreat anyone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't because they were merely passing through, they got drinks from us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That clarifies the matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sir, while you were in Arapusa, could you freely moved or were you ordered by authorities to stay in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: There was a kind of a protocol, and yes, they gave it to us, since there were two guards in the village, Gornji and Donji Petrovic, then they told us that we could not walk in twos, that only those who were representatives of village could get out and go into the town to talk with the relevant commander, that is policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I intentionally used only word authorities. Who were these authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: The Serb authorities, of course. Their chief staff, and their headquarters was in Jasenica, in Arapusa was only the police, and some troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And on 1st of May, you move to Sanski Most; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move straight away to his knowledge, what he could tell us about the accused. I think that's the substance of his testimony basically.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sir, I intended to show you some documents but these documents are straightforward and, as you pointed out yesterday, you will read all the exhibits, so I don't need to tender them through this witness. Sir, can you tell us whether you know Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes. I know Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin rather superficially. We were not close. But we -- there was an occasion when we were introduced to each other directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By whom? By whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When and by whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic introduced us in Banja Luka at a time of a match we were playing there and we were in the Intercontinental Hotel. We were playing a match and the delegation which came with Mr. Klickovic, Mr. Brdjanin was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: It was in the autumn of 1991. Roughly. I mean, I can't remember exactly. But it had to be Saturday or Sunday because that's where matches were played.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In 1992, during the year 1992, did you see him again, maybe on television? Did you attend any rallies, which he would attend?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: At that rally, Mr. Brdjanin was portrayed as an entrepreneur, as a good head of family, and that we can talk to him when it came to cooperation with -- between our two teams. When -- once I was deported, when I came to Sanski Most, I saw Mr. Brdjanin twice on TV.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And can you tell us now very briefly what you remember you saw on TV with respect to Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: It was some sort of a public rally and Mr. Brdjanin was addressing the people and talking about the situation in Banja Luka. The impression that I got from that speech was different. We were watching this rally on TV, and he was very extremist in his appearance, very much against Muslims, against neighbours, and he said that Serbs should not be influenced by anybody and that they shouldn't lose. Why, he said, because they can always be stabbed in the back by Muslims in Banja Luka and in other places. The picture that I had of him before was something totally different. So I was very much disappointed and very much surprised with what I heard him saying on TV that second time around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned two times you saw him on television, no? And was it the same thing, same story, on both occasions or was this only on one of these TV transmissions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the first time. And the second time I saw him as participating in a meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go to the second now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second time I saw him, he also addressed the people who were there and he talked about the attitude that should be adopted towards Muslims and citizens of Banja Luka in general. Again, he used very strong words and the attitude again was the same. He stressed the same things. He said that Muslims could not stay in Banja Luka, that their safety and security should be dealt with in other ways, primarily by moving them out. And this meeting was a meeting of -- not many people. And I saw that on Serbian TV. So this was soon after, a few days after. I was in Sanski Most for 12 days. So these two appearances came within a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think we can break here. Mr. Cunningham, how -- do you think you will need the entire last session for your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will resume in 20 minutes' time if that is --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would really appreciate if we could finish this witness today because.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm go to impress on Mr. Cunningham the need to finish this witness today but that would mean you stopping basically here. I mean I think there is enough material -- in fact, I don't think we need to go any further than what we have already and we can start with the cross-examination. That's unless -- I don't want to stop you, Ms. Richterova, if you do have some important additional questions that you would like to put, do tell me and I'm sure that we can find some cooperation from Mr. Cunningham too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: He will tell you right after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have only one document which I want to show the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You have a document in front of you, it is P2094. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we have that, I think, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, you have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we go to private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are now going to be cross-examined by Mr. Cunningham. Please make sure that you answer each question that he puts to you as fully and as truthfully as you can just as you did with the questions coming from the Prosecution. Can I count on you, Mr. Cunningham, that we will concentrate on what is important and finish by quarter to 2.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I will concentrate on what is important, as to whether we will finish by quarter to 2.00, I can't guarantee that to the Court but I'll do my best and I certainly don't have any problem if I'm close to the end I'll inform the Court and if it's suitable with your staff and the interpreters to work a little late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No one likes that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm the leader of that group, believe me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, let's get it over. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I want to make sure that you have access to the statements that you have provided to the Prosecution. Are those -- I'd ask the Prosecutor whether those statements are available to this witness? The statements I'm talking about are his statement to the AID 26 August, 1992, his diary, his first statement to the OTP on 27 August, 1999, the second statement to the OTP, 13 February, 2001. Sir, before you testified today, at any time before your trial -- this trial, did you have an opportunity to review each and every one of those statements that you made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Remembering His Honour's statements to you about answering the questions concisely, I'm going to ask you questions that call for yes or no answers and try to do that as best as you can. The first statement I'm going to talk to you about is your statement that you made to AID 26 August, 1992. You have that statement in front of you and you have reviewed it according to your prior testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, there is absolutely nothing in that statement about Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes. I would agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You have provided the OTP with a 72-page diary that recounts the events in April of 1992. You have read that; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: There is no mention of the defendant in that statement that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: No, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The very first statement that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor was on 27 August, 1999; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And in that statement, there is absolutely no mention of the defendant again; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: You're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The statement of --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Didn't understand you, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Find your statement dated 27 August, 1999.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes, now I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That is a statement you've read and you would agree with me, wouldn't you, sir, that it's only in -- even in this statement there is no mention of the defendant; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Correct. There isn't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. It is on 13 February, 2001, only after the defendant is indicted that you introduce him into your statements; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And in that statement, you say that you met him -- actually you say that you saw him at a sporting event; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, you met with Ms. Richterova, the Prosecutor, before your testimony and provided her with additional information about the defendant; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: When it comes to this statement and introduction of this gentleman, that was part of the procedure of drafting this new statement. That's when I introduced this meeting between Mr. Brdjanin and Mr. Klickovic and that's the way I extended my statement. I spoke about the way we met. I was actually surprised when I heard that I might appear here as a witness for the Prosecution against Mr. Brdjanin, given the fact that my knowledge of him was rather superficial.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You had absolutely no idea that you were coming to testify in his trial?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't know that I would appear as a witness because the whole procedure, the whole process, started in 1992 when I gave my first statement and it lasted up to now, up to the time when I arrived here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When you come to The Hague, all of a sudden, you have new information about the defendant, and that new information is not only did you see him at a sporting event but you were introduced to him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly what I said. It took place at the International Hotel when we played that game. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there because I don't have much time and I know you would like to get home for the weekend. Here is my point: How is it that you remember this stuff and bring up this new information about a personal meeting the day before trial?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean? One moment. He spoke about the meeting he had with Radoslav Brdjanin when he was introduced by Klickovic in his statement of the 13th February of 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I believe he said that he saw him at a sporting event. There was nothing about a personal introduction in there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I think he just confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. So when did you confirm the first time to the Prosecution that you actually was -- you had Brdjanin introduced to you or you were introduced to Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the International Hotel when we were having lunch, as a team, as a group of athletes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Between 13th February, 2001, and when you arrived here in The Hague to give testimony, did you have any contacts of any manner with the Prosecution, particularly with regard to your testimony or with regard to testifying in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the 13th February, 2001, I'm afraid I have not understood you properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were you -- after you made the statement of the 13th February, 2001, were you in contact with the Office of the Prosecutor regarding the -- your coming over here to give evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When was that? When did you learn that you were coming over here to give evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I learned that last month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Last month. And were you told in which trial you would be testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And when you arrived here and you were briefed by, interviewed by, again by the officer from the office of the Prosecution, you made this additional statement about Radoslav Brdjanin being introduced to you by Klickovic sometime in 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you make this statement arising out of a specific question or was it just your spontaneous contribution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave that statement in a conversation, when I was asked whether I knew Mr. Brdjanin and that's when I gave the statement the way I did, and I said that I knew him superficially, that I had a meeting with him, that I was introduced to him, and that I was disappointed when I saw him again on TV in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And the obvious question that has been put to you is: Why, when -- why, when you were interviewed on the 13th February, 2001, you did not mention to the Prosecution that you had actually met Radoslav Brdjanin? Why did you just say that you had seen him, that you knew that he was a friend of Klickovic, without mentioning that you had actually been introduced to him by Klickovic himself? Why did you omit to mention that in the course of your 13 February, 2001 statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. It must have been spontaneously. That's the way the conversation was conducted. Nobody asked me to provide them with any details. I just spoke the way I did. It was a superficial question and it called for a superficial answer, and that's exactly what I gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Chamber is satisfied with his reply, Mr. Cunningham, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In a document handed to me today by the Prosecutor entitled supplemental information sheet, this is what the Prosecutor told me as a result of her meeting with you. She says that the witness states that Gojko Klickovic introduced the defendant to the witness during a sporting event in 1991 and it was in Bosanska Krupa. That's what the information provided me by the Prosecutor says. Here is my question: In your testimony today, you say that you met him in Banja Luka. Had you seen him in Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him in Bosanska Krupa and that is the first time I saw him. But as I was a student in Banja Luka, we often played games there and I would see him there amongst his associates. The two of us both had a large circle of friends and that's how I sort of knew him by sight. I knew him superficially but never was introduced to him before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. Remember I don't have much time and you want to go home so answer the question as best as you can. You told us, yes or no, you've seen him in Bosanska Krupa. When? What year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: I believe that this was in 1990. There was a, again, a game and it was played at the stadium in Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you if you know Esad Velic and his brother. Do you know who they are?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Esad Velic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know both of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it still doesn't work. Let's redact this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour I was doing my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I believe you can go ahead and answer now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Thank you. As to why they didn't see him, it has to do with a specific nature of our meeting. Gojko Klickovic was my associate in the same team. He was the vice-president of that team and (Redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whenever we played those matches, these two persons never attended any of those matches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Full stop. That's your explanation. Try to answer the question. We are not interested on who Gojko Klickovic was, whether he was your associate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Judge, this is very important for me. I would ask those questions about those matches in my questions so I think it's better to ask it now. I think it's important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Cunningham. And we are in open session so no names of protected witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want to talk to you now about an organisation that you've talked about in your statements that were introduced and it's called the club of intellectuals and I take it that one of the things that the club did was to discuss the political events of the day in Bosanska Krupa. My question is: Is that right? Did you talk about the political events in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes, sometime.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And in the course of your dealings at the club of intellectuals, you had dealings with Mr. Klickovic that we have talked about; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And another individual by the name of Vjestica and I'm apologising for my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during the time that you were in the club of intellectuals and a resident of your municipality, you had the opportunity to have many dealings first of all with Mr. Klickovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Only in the field of athletics, not in any other field.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Isn't it true that you attended meetings where Mr. Klickovic was representing the SDS in April of 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes. This was a joint meeting in the hotel with citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And also, Mr. Vjestica was present at this joint meeting with the citizens there; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And the purpose for those meetings, this meeting, was to try to avert a conflict in your municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And at this meeting, the two people who were representing the SDS, Mr. Klickovic and Mr. Vjestica, made certain representations to the crowd about their connections?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Klickovic -- let me back up. At the meeting, you told us in the statement that the SDS made guarantees that the political matters would be handled by high-ranking officials in Sarajevo and Bosanska Krupa would not be affected by aggressive acts. Did they say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: At this meeting, Vjestica said that he would influence the top; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I believe it was at a meeting on April 18 where Klickovic and others said that they had political connections that they could use to prevent an attack on your municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Correct. Adding that Krupa would be the last one if a war started.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And you wanted to believe them when they -- believe Klickovic and Vjestica when they made these representations to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: I did, because that was a promise given to us and the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: So they led to you believe they had political connections that could avoid conflict; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And they told you this even, I believe, up to the day before or the day of the attack; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: They said it then and the attack ensued three days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And you felt totally betrayed by what they told you; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Why, of course, because we had been deceived.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you ever think that in addition to deceiving you about there would be no attack, did you ever think that he was deceiving you about their supposed connections with people at the top?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: No. Because we believed that they really had connections at the top, because previous visits of the Serb top-most authorities -- of the Serb top-most authorities to Bosanska Krupa had already taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. You believed that -- you believed them when they said that conflict was avoided; right? That conflict could be avoided; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That turned out to be a lie.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. I want to talk with you about various statements that you made in your statement to the OTP that is in evidence and that's the statement February 13th, 2001. I invite you to have that statement ready in case you need to look at it. One of the things that you talk about is you make a statement in there and I apologise, I don't have the exact page number, but you're talking about either Klickovic or Vjestica having a connection with Karadzic. Do you remember making a statement like that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will read out to him the relative parts because that's how we do it usually. I am reading from your own statement, sir. As mentioned earlier, Vjestica said he would influence the top, without naming anyone, and try to arrange something so that Bosanska Krupa would be the last attacked. Three days later, Bosanska Krupa was attacked which in my opinion is betrayal. It became obvious after the events the person he was supposed to try and influence was Radovan Karadzic. Then you continue saying, "I know that Banja Luka had to have an influence in these decisions."

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Here is -- when you're done reading that, let me know. Here is my question: You make a conclusion that the person he was supposed to try and influence was Karadzic. Do you have any real evidence, any documents, any proof, other than your conclusion, about this connection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Well, we thought it was logical because we knew that Karadzic was on that top but before that, Mrs. Plavsic visited Bosanska Krupa too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: My question was very simple. Do you have any documents, any physical evidence, to show this connection from your municipality to Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: No, no. I don't have that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: At the same part of that statement you also say Banja Luka had to have an influence over these events and His Honour read that to you and I want to ask you questions about that statement. Are you aware of any documents that the Prosecutor has or that anyone in Bosanska Krupa that shows the defendant giving an order to Vjestica or Klickovic to do any of the things that they were responsible in your municipality? Do you have any documents like that or aware of any documents like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: I personally, as a witness, do not have such documents and I'm not abreast of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In your statement, and you say Vjestica and Klickovic cooperated closely with Pale and Banja Luka. You remember making that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you think the two men that I just talked about, Vjestica and Klickovic, do you think on their own that they were capable of doing the things that happened in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: At the time when we used to live together, I wouldn't have believed that they would be up to anything like that. I mean prior to the attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think he has understood your question, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: If the Court wishes to rephrase it otherwise I'll be glad to give it a try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you happy with his answer? I don't think he answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I don't think he did either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sir, look at me. It's not your fault. It's -- I realise that after three hours sitting there or I don't know how long, it becomes tiring for everyone. We are talking of the events not when you were living together in harmony but when things went wrong. And Mr. Cunningham wants to know Mr. Klickovic and Mr. Vjestica all of a sudden they took certain decisions and took certain attitudes and took certain actions. His question is: Do you believe that they had enough or sufficient power to be able to do that on their own or were they being orchestrated or directed by others? In other words, that they did not have a free hand, they had to do what others told them to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first part, the arrests, one could feel that they were waiting to get something from somebody. I mean, and I'm talking about the fate of one -- of 1200 of us prisoners there prior to the deportation. But on the other hand, they did play the main role in all the events that took place in Bosanska Krupa. There is no doubt about that. And I also can give you an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 30th of April, when we were to be deported to Agici and then that sudden change to send us to Sanski Most, I was allowed by them to go to Jasenica as a delegation from the Arapusa camp (Redacted) (Redacted) So that our discussion when we went to him was more or less at that level so I asked him why was I captured, and at the end, (Redacted) (Redacted) and so on and so forth and I'm also a blood donor and 14 -- before that I donated my blood to a Serb to save him. So I told 14 him, "After all that why have I been arrested?" And he said, (Redacted) this was a -- this was a mistake because we -- I am a Serb, you're a Muslim and we are enemies."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are -- I understand this is Klickovic, no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Vjestica, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to redact from several parts, if you print his answer entirely I will indicate to you which parts need to be redacted. Again you were not careful. You mentioned your name, you mentioned who was your neighbour. Any way, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to talk to you and I'm not doing this to confuse you. There is an area I want to talk to you about and that involves another portion of the events prior to the assault and that has to do with whether or not the local Muslims were armed. The defence of the city was offered by the police and the reserve police; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: You are.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And there were Bosniak citizens who assisted in that defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And at the time of the assault, you were a member of the club of intellectuals; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'd like to have the witness, with the help of the usher, see defendant Brdjanin's Exhibits 142A and B. I've given Ms. Chuqing copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: If you could give a copy to the Prosecution? There is a set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of it as yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm tendering it now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. This will be tendered and accepted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if we are going to mention names, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You direct me Mr. Cunningham if we need to go into private.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, in private session, please, as a matter of caution because I'm going to question him about a written statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's go again to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: My question is do you remember telling us about that? Do you remember, roughly speaking, what month and what year that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: It was roughly between the 3rd and the 7th, thereabouts, but before Kozarac, before the attack on Kozarac. It is then that I remember Mr. Brdjanin speaking on television, because we were already in a basement watching television.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The 3rd and the 7th of what month, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: May, May.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what town or municipality were you in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: In Naprelje which is Sanski Most, in the village of Naprelje.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I promise this is the last area. The second time you saw him on TV you said that I believe it was at a rally of some sort. Do you know where the rally was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: No. I can't recall but it was on television again, and he was at that particular moment, when we were watching, I recognised him and that is how we reacted to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What municipality were you in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: Sanski Most was the municipality and the village was Naprelje.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what month was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT55
utterances.text: That was May again, sometime between the 14th and the 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: May I have just a moment, judge and I think I'm done and I think I took less than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, I have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No there is no re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And there are no questions from our side as well. I wish to take this opportunity to thank you, sir, for having come over to give testimony in this case. I thank you in my own name and I also thank you on behalf of Judge Janu and Judge Taya who sit with me in this case. You will now be escorted out of the courtroom by the usher and given all the assistance you require to enable you to return home. And on behalf of everyone in this courtroom, I wish you a safe journey back home, thank you. Before we adjourn, two things. Mr. Cunningham, if you could impress on Mr. Ackerman the need to have the responses ready by Monday if possible on those 92 bis, remaining 92 bis --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's working on them?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: No, I'm working on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So thank you. And last thing is I should like to publicly thank the interpreters, the technicians and everyone present in this courtroom, mentioned or unmentioned, I'm probably not aware of everyone. Thank you so much for your indulgence and for your cooperation which made it possible for this gentleman to be able to return home to his family this weekend and not next week. Thank you.
